paragraphs.text: A sport known simply as the Ball Game featured in the mythology and history of ancient Mesoamerica, a geographical and cultural area extending from what is now central Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Costa Rica. The Ball Game was an important element in the myth of the Mesoamerican gods Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu. These two brothers annoyed the other gods with their noisy play and were deceived into competing with them in a ball game. The other gods won and Hun Hunahpu lost his head as a consequence.

In fact, some evidence shows that a ball game like this existed, but no one knows exactly when it was invented. Apparently, it was first played in Mesoamerica at some time during the Pre-classical Period (2500-100 BC). It became a popular pastime in all of Mesoamerica and eventually was exported to North America and other cultures in the Caribbean area. It was usually played on courts in the district of a city used as the centre for religious rituals, a fact that suggests that the game was regarded as more significant than just a sport.

In a famous legend, which may have been based on historical events, a ball game was held in what is now Mexico at the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan between the rival kings Motecuhzoma Xocoyotzin (circa 1502–1520 AD) and king Nezahualpilli. Nezahualpilli had predicted that Motecuhzoma’s kingdom would fall, and a ball game between teams of the two rulers was set up to establish the truth of this bold prophecy. Motecuhzoma’s side lost the match and it is a historical fact that he did in the end lose his kingdom at the hands of invaders.

The first courts where the ball games were held were rectangular surfaces of flattened earth. During later periods the courts remained the same shape, but were set between two parallel stone side walls. These could be perpendicular or sloping away from the players. The ends of the courts could be defined by walls or, in some cases, the ends were just indicated by markers on the ground and left open. Each side wall typically had a large vertical ring made of stone placed high up it.

There are many surviving courts, with 11 found in El Tajin in Mexico, which may have been the most significant centre of the Ball Game in its day. Different courts appear to have been of a range of dimensions, but the remains of a court in El Tajin is 60 metres long and this seems to have been typical. The largest surviving court can be seen at the city of Chichen Itza, also in Mexico, and is 146 metres long and 36 metres wide.

The balls could be lethal if they struck a player as they were fashioned from rubber which was very hard. They measured anywhere from 10 to 30 centimetres in diameter and weighed from 500 grams to 3.5 kilograms. Remarkably, seven balls have been preserved in the boggy wetlands of El Manati near the Olmec city of San Lorenzo on Mexico’s Gulf coast. These preserved balls range from 8 to 25 centimetres in diameter and date from between 1600 and 1200 BC.

The exact rules of the game are unknown today and in all probability there were variations across the cultures and in the different periods in which it was played. However, the main aim apparently was to get the ball through one of the stone rings. This was more difficult than it might appear, as players were not allowed to touch the ball with their hands. It seems that good players became highly skilled at directing the ball with their elbows, knees, thighs and shoulders. There was also an alternative version, where the ball was struck with sticks, but this was not as widespread.

Teams were composed of two or three players and were made up exclusively of males. Players could be professionals or amateurs, and there is evidence of betting on the outcome of important games. The game also had strong associations with wars, and those captured in battle were often forced to play the game. Players were frequently depicted in Mesoamerican art, appearing in sculptures, ceramics and architectural decoration — the latter often decorating the courts themselves. These depictions often show the players dressed in protective gear such as padding for the hips, knees, elbows and wrists. The players shown in these works of art also typically have a helmet with grills across the face.

Winners of the game received various trophies, many of which have been excavated at archaeological sites. Some were representations of the human head with a handle attached, and others took the form of an arm, a hand or a bird with a fan-like tail. All of these are frequently found in graves from the period.
